title: SYSK Selects: How Revisionist History Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of a Stuff You Should Know episode, introduced by Chuck, about revisionist history. The hosts open with Fanta Orange's origins as a Coca-Cola product created in Nazi Germany during the war embargo, then turn to the George Washington cherry tree fable and Mason Weems. They discuss Columbus Day and the Pocahontas-John Smith legend, then define revisionism and its three lenses: theoretical (social/cultural), fact-checking, and negative/political. The Thomas Jefferson and Sally Hemings DNA evidence is used as an example. The episode traces modern revisionism from the Marxist coinage of the term, through World War I, Carl Becker's 1931 AHA speech, the League of Nations textbook guidelines, the World War II "age of historical consensus," and the 1960s shift toward inclusive history (political, economic, racial, sexual lenses, Charles Beard). It covers how textbooks get revised, the influence of Texas, the backlash against revisionism (Bush 2003 remarks, Florida 2006 law), the difference between revisionism and negationism, and how to spot crackpot history such as Gavin Menzies' Chinese-discovery claim. The episode closes with a listener mail about handwriting analysis and a call for teacher feedback.

segments.title: Chuck's pick and the Fanta Orange Nazi soda question
segments.summary: Chuck introduces his pick of Revisionist History. Josh and Chuck discuss whether Fanta Orange is a Nazi soda, concluding it was created by a Coca-Cola Germany employee during the war embargo and enjoyed by Nazis, unlike products such as Volkswagen, while IBM's wartime role in Germany is cited as true.

segments.title: George Washington and the cherry tree myth
segments.summary: The hosts recount the cherry tree fable about George Washington and explain it was invented by biographer Mason Locke Weems. They note it was taught as fact in textbooks until it was removed around 2008 after no evidence of cherry trees on the Washington family home was found.

segments.title: Columbus and Columbus Day
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck criticize Columbus's treatment of Indigenous people and say Columbus Day is likely to decline. Chuck mentions a teacher friend in Portland who teaches a revised version of Columbus history.

segments.title: Objective versus subjective history
segments.summary: The hosts explain that historians in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries came to see history as subjective and evolving rather than objective, and that revisionism is not necessarily a dirty word. They introduce three perspectives on revisionism.

segments.title: Three lenses of revisionism and the Jefferson example
segments.summary: The three lenses are theoretical (social perspective), fact-checking, and negative/political revisionism. Thomas Jefferson and Sally Hemings are used as an example, with DNA evidence in the late 1990s confirming children together, which ended the negative view that it was a rumor.

segments.title: Origins of modern revisionism: WWI, Becker and the League of Nations
segments.summary: The term revisionist history was coined by Marxists decades before World War I and gained wider use afterward. Historians came to see history as subjective; Carl Becker said so in an American Historical Association speech. The Treaty of Versailles blamed Germany, later documents showed other factors, and the League of Nations issued textbook guidelines.

segments.title: Age of historical consensus and the 1960s shift
segments.summary: After World War II, historians reached an age of consensus emphasizing American victory. The 1960s upheaval (Vietnam, civil rights, feminism) led historians to tell everyone's story through political, economic, racial, and sexual lenses. Charles Beard's economic interpretation of the Constitution is discussed, along with the omission of Native Americans, Malcolm X, and women from school curricula.

segments.title: Japanese American camps and zero-sum history
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how the Japanese American incarceration camps entered textbooks in the 1990s, honoring the victims but reflecting poorly on the U.S. government. They note that revising history often has a zero-sum effect. Harriet Tubman and Elizabeth Cady Stanton are mentioned as examples of women in history.

segments.title: Pocahontas myth and how history gets corrected
segments.summary: The hosts describe history as a game of telephone and use the Disney Pocahontas story as an example: Pocahontas was about eleven when Smith was in Jamestown, and she later married John Rolfe and died around age twenty-one. Declassified documents and forensic science are cited as ways history gets corrected, including the CIA's LSD testing and the Star Wars program.
topics: Star Wars program and Cold War

segments.title: Textbook revision, Texas influence and the backlash
segments.summary: The hosts explain the slow, multi-step process of revising textbooks, the outsized influence of Texas as a large buyer, and the Institute for International Textbook Research. They discuss pushback on the AHA national history standards and Bush's 2003 use of 'revisionist history' for media coverage, and Florida's 2006 law restricting such teaching. They distinguish revisionism from negationism and give a checklist for spotting crackpot theories such as Gavin Menzies' Chinese-discovery claim.

segments.title: Listener mail on handwriting analysis
segments.summary: A forensic document examiner praises the handwriting analysis episode, describing their work with travel and identity documents and a Secret Service threat-letter database.

segments.title: Sign-off and call for teacher feedback
segments.summary: The hosts ask teachers to email ideas on fixing public education and sign off with contact information.
